title_original: Leica Oskar Barnack Award (LOBA) 2026 & LOBA Women Grant
excerpt_original: Damir Faizulin has won the main category of the Leica Oskar Barnack Award (LOBA), Laila AnnMarie Stevens has been honored in the Newcomer category, […] Cet article Leica Oskar Barnack Award (LOBA) 2026 & LOBA Women Grant est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: Damir Faizulin has won the main category of the Leica Oskar Barnack Award (LOBA) , Laila AnnMarie Stevens has been honored in the Newcomer category, and Valentina Sinis is the happy recipient of the LOBA Women Grant . Once again this year, the award ceremony will be a highlight of the Celebration of Photography evening taking place on October 8 at the Leica Welt in Wetzlar.

The two winning series of the 46th LOBA convinced the five members of the jury, who made their selection from more than 400 submissions. For the main category, more than 130 specialists from the international photography scene, from some fifty countries, submitted their recommendations. The Leica Oskar Barnack Award Newcomer was awarded in collaboration with 28 institutions and universities in 18 countries. As for the new LOBA Women Grant, the decision was made after reviewing the many freely submitted applications presenting project ideas in detail.

Awarded since 1980, the LOBA is today one of the world’s most renowned and generously endowed distinctions in the field of photography: the LOBA winner receives €40,000 as well as Leica photography equipment worth €10,000, while the Newcomer Award winner receives €10,000 and a Leica Q3. The LOBA Women Grant carries a prize of €10,000. In addition, the selected candidate receives a Leica Q3 and benefits from professional support throughout the execution and production of her project.
Damir Faizulin: Preserving Nature as Preserving Ourselves
Winner of the Leica Oskar Barnack Award 2026

In his award-winning series, the Russian photographer presents the nature and living conditions of the mountains of Dagestan, a republic in the North Caucasus, in southern Russia. Amid current changes, the arrival of tourism, modern architecture, and the erosion of established structures and culture, Damir Faizulin’s images point to the threats weighing on the fragile balance between the local population and nature, while paying tribute to the beauty of the region.

Quote from Damir Faizulin: “I first went to Dagestan in 2020 as a tourist, and I immediately felt deep within me a connection with the cultural codes of this place, with the awareness of the moment, and with my personal interest in the subject. I had a feeling that the region was going to change very quickly in the near future, and I wanted to document these changes. That is why I moved to Dagestan in 2021, in order to explore the region in depth. For me, it is important that a photo does not simplify reality, but helps us identify its complexity.”

Damir Faizulin was born in Uzbekistan in 1986. After the fall of the Soviet Union, his family settled in Russia. Damir Faizulin pursued a successful career in combat sports and as a professional wrestler until his retirement at the age of 33. He subsequently took part in photography workshops led by photojournalist Dmitry Markov in Kaliningrad. Since 2020, he has been carrying out his own projects. The LOBA is the first international competition he has entered.
Laila AnnMarie Stevens: Clayton Sisterhood Project
Leica Oskar Barnack Award Newcomer 2026

Inspired by a desire to remember her ancestors, the American photographer explores in her black-and-white series present-day queer family relationships and the still-living legacy of strong, determined Black women. Her series centers on the way of life created by the photographer’s two sisters and four nieces. All six left Queens, New York, to settle together in a house with land in Clayton, North Carolina.

Quote from Laila AnnMarie Stevens: “When I selected these photos, my wish was for them to reflect the varied forms through which intergenerational bonds are expressed. That my work is receiving such recognition gives me a great deal of courage. I place great hope in this award, particularly in view of the current political climate in the United States, where many rights relating to autonomy, caring for others, and visibility are being actively called into question.”

Laila AnnMarie Stevens was born in 2001 in South Jamaica, in the New York borough of Queens, and began being published at the age of 20 in the “Metropolitan” section of The New York Times . Since then, her work has been seen in numerous renowned publications. She holds a Bachelor of Fine Arts in photography and media from the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York.
Valentina Sinis: The Last Butterflies
LOBA Women Grant 2026/2027

This award enables the Italian photographer to continue the long-term project she is carrying out in Iraqi Kurdistan, where she is focusing on Kurdish women who left their lands to join the armed resistance. Through portraits, landscapes and abandoned places, the photographer opens a new chapter in which she examines how combat shapes and alters ties to a country and to family, as well as the sense of belonging, and shows the human cost of these fighters’ commitment. The fruits of this new chapter will be presented at the 2027 LOBA.

Italian photographer Valentina Sinis lives and works between China, Iraq and Italy. Through her remarkable work, she draws close to the realities of everyday life and to people the media do not generally talk about. Her photographs have already been published in numerous international newspapers and magazines.
Quote from Karin Rehn-Kaufmann:

“‘The Last Butterflies’ is a masterful demonstration of the new role women have taken on in war for some time now. These photographs show clearly and movingly their shared struggle for their country, without men. It is important that Valentina Sinis be able to continue and complete this project.”
Quotes from the LOBA 2026 jury:

Karin Rehn-Kaufmann: “On behalf of the entire LOBA 2026 jury (Jane’a Johnson, curator and researcher, exhibition assistant, Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), New York (United States); Celina Lunsford, artistic director and curator of the FFF, Fotografie Forum Frankfurt (Germany); Paolo Pellegrin, photographer (Italy); Gu Zheng, professor at the School of Journalism, Fudan University, Shanghai (China)), I warmly congratulate the winners.”

The jury “had intense discussions, and that is precisely what gives this process its strength,” says Karin Rehn-Kaufmann. “We had fascinating exchanges about the photographers’ integrity, their stories, and of course the visual result,” adds Celina Lunsford. “The quality of the work was high, as were our expectations.” Jane’a Johnson agrees: “The discussions were lively, deep, and always marked by respect. Each of us brought our own point of view. The atmosphere was very collegial, and we ended up truly building a bond among ourselves.” Reflecting on this year’s edition, Karin Rehn-Kaufmann notes: “As is so often the case, I was struck by the variety of subjects addressed. The styles were also very different: from classic documentary approaches to poetic and experimental narratives. This year, the selection struck me as particularly varied and nuanced. We were more interested in long-term questions and in the depth of photographic research than in quick visual effect.”

“You can’t imagine how much this award means,” stresses Jane’a Johnson. “It is a real financial boon for photographers, it gives them access to quality equipment and creates a link with the legacy of some of the greatest photographers who have ever held a camera.” Thus the LOBA ranks today among the world’s most widely recognized awards: “Whether I’m attending a photography festival or doing research, renowned photographers know this award,” observes Celina Lunsford, before continuing: “Today, the list of finalists also provides an excellent overview for curators, festival directors and editors.”
Comments on the two winning series:

Karin Rehn-Kaufmann: “Damir Faizulin’s series ‘Preserving Nature as Preserving Ourselves’ beautifully illustrates the close link between the well-being of humanity and the state of our natural environment. His calm, composed, and at times humorous style allows him to address, with sensitivity and nuance, one of the most urgent issues of our time. The photographs invite us to reflect on our responsibility toward nature and to rethink the relationship between humans and the environment.

“The series forms a visual whole that is particularly striking. It reconciles documentary precision with a poetic style and includes photographs that move us just as much as they invite reflection. And it is precisely this balance between the relevance of the subject and emotional depth that gives this work its distinctiveness.”

Karin Rehn-Kaufmann: “With the ‘Clayton Sisterhood Project,’ Laila AnnMarie Stevens delivers an intimate and authentic body of work centered on community, belonging, and bonds among women. She shows kindness, respect, and sensitivity in telling the resilience and strength of a community. The series explicitly shows that solidarity and interpersonal ties can be a source of strength and hope.”

Exhibition and catalog: The LOBA 2026 catalog accompanies the exhibition at the Ernst Leitz Museum. It presents all the finalists’ series together with interviews and contextual material. After the exhibition in Wetzlar, the LOBA 2026 works will travel to Leica galleries and photography festivals around the world.
More information about this year’s winners is available at: www.leica-oskar-barnack-award.com .
